book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality

chapters.relation: William Irwin's editor introduction tells how a tape of "N.I.B." stopping at "My name is Lucifer, please take my hand" hooked him at thirteen, and argues Sabbath deserve serious philosophy: their riffs and lyrics confront existential despair, war, drugs, and the nature of evil in shades of gray rather than Satanism. It frames the book's guiding questions (what makes Sabbath sound evil, is evil in the ear of the beholder, is it still Sabbath without Ozzy) and promises that philosophers can deepen our listening to Ozzy, Tony, Geezer, and Bill without recovering authorial intent.

William Irwin reads the Ozzy-era catalog as unwitting British existentialism: "Johnny Blade", "Paranoid", and "Wheels of Confusion" voice Camus's absurd, the mismatch between our desires and a world where life has no meaning and "hell is other people" explains why Iron Man, saved yet treated as a mindless thing, plans vengeance. The chapter argues the band moves from despair toward freedom and self-creation: "Supernaut" and "Under the Sun" reject religion in the spirit of Nietzsche's death of God, "Cornucopia" depicts bad-faith conformity to plastic suburban lives, and "Children of the Grave" plus Sabbath's own music-making exemplify the claim that artistic creativity is the proper response to pain, with the fan invited to sculpt himself into an authentic individual Sisyphus-style.

Liz Stillwaggon Swan surveys Sabbath's pictures of moral evil (nuclear annihilation in "Electric Funeral", heroin's "deadly pin" in "Hand of Doom", social oppression allegorized as the Satan of "Black Sabbath") and argues the band poses the problem of evil without solving it theologically. Against the view that invoking evil presupposes God, she aligns Sabbath with Augustine's rejection of Manichaean evil-as-a-force, reading evil as a privation traceable to free human choices, and with Bertrand Russell's "A Free Man's Worship": "Children of the Grave", "Into the Void", "Spiral Architect", and "Symptom of the Universe" urge that we defeat evil by imagining and building a better possible reality through love, vegan-pacifist Geezer Butler being the living proof behind the stage persona.

Brian Froese argues Black Sabbath's occult imagery expresses an eschatological imagination forged in the rubble of working-class, postwar Birmingham as a rebuke to hippie utopianism. Songs like "Black Sabbath", "War Pigs" (originally "Walpurgis"), and "Electric Funeral" borrow the literary devices of the Book of Revelation, Satan, final judgment, cosmic journeys, as what Elaine Pagels calls war literature for a Cold War and Vietnam world, while "Iron Man" transvalues the Christian savior into a resurrected anti-hero and "After Forever" and "Lord of this World" both embrace and resent the faith. He concludes the band built a sacralized, contradictory, fatalistic cosmology in which "the chosen one" cannot escape his fate, reworking Christian apocalypse for the industrial marginalized.

Joel McIver, drawing on years of interviewing the band, argues the sinister sound is psychoacoustics rather than Satan: Iommi's lower tuning adopted after the sheet-metal press took his fingertips, the tritone or diabolus in musica that anchors "Black Sabbath", horror-film tremolo, minor keys, Ozzy's untrained monotone, and Bill Ward's slightly dragged, jazzy beats, artistic imperfections that keep the music lifelike. Against Schopenhauer's view that music directly expresses universal emotions, so the tritone would naturally sound like discord to anyone, McIver contends the devil's interval is a Western convention that only became inseparable from evil once Sabbath fused it with Geezer's occult lyrics and nightmare cover art.

James Heathers asks why the most improbable band became the one true originator of heavy metal and answers with Schopenhauer: industrial Aston, Birmingham was a monument to the ceaseless, unsatisfied striving of the Will, and music, which maps directly onto the Will itself, gave that world its voice. The tritone's numerically hideous ratios, a point traced through Rameau back to Pythagoras, make it the natural interval of morbidity, which is why "Black Sabbath" and everything from Liszt's Dante Sonata to death metal is marinated in it, and why doom was not a predictable development like Deep Purple or Led Zeppelin. He closes on the irony that Schopenhauer, who preached ascetic denial of the Will, would have loathed a band that answered factory-town despair by smothering the Will in lager, hash, cocaine, and women, only to breed more want in the worst of all possible worlds.

Ken Pepper uses Merleau-Ponty's Phenomenology of Perception to explain how Tony Iommi's homemade plastic fingertips work: like the blind man's cane, they are incorporated into his body schema so that he perceives the fretboard through them, refuting the Cartesian "objective body" picture on which playing would be inner plans causing finger movements. On creative freedom, the chapter stages Merleau-Ponty against Sartre's radical freedom, Iommi did choose to relearn guitar after hearing two-fingered Django Reinhardt, and his restricted two-finger chords, lighter strings, and drop tunings birthed heavy metal, but Sartre is wrong that attitude alone transcends disability, since some possibilities (playing at all without the tips) were simply not live. Only Iommi, taking up the possibilities his body-in-his-situation afforded, could have invented metal.

Greg Littmann imagines Aristotle auditioning for Black Sabbath in 1970 to argue the band satisfies the Poetics and Politics: music that gives pleasure, even the "perverted modes" working-class audiences enjoy, is legitimate art, and Sabbath's darkness works as catharsis, purging fear and pity as Greek tragedy did through Oedipus, the doomed figure in black of "Black Sabbath", the betrayed and ignored Iron Man, and the hopeless narrator of "Paranoid". Songs like "War Pigs", "Electric Funeral", and "Children of the Grave" also do what Aristotle says poetry does better than history, imagining alternative futures that spur citizens to political thought, while the band's drug lore maps onto the Aristotelian mean: beer and a little weed yes, heroin and cocaine never, and Ozzy's firing shows the price of intemperance.

Søren Frimodt-Møller argues that heavy metal cannot be defined by necessary and sufficient conditions, down-tuning, distortion, growls, and double-kick each fail as criteria, and that genres instead work like Wittgenstein's family-resemblance concepts, learned by actual cases the way words are learned in language games. The family of metal begins with Black Sabbath as prototype: he traces doom to "Black Sabbath" and "War Pigs", thrash to "Paranoid" and "Symptom of the Universe" (compare "Master of Puppets"), progressive and power metal to the Dio-era records that influenced Iron Maiden, and grunge to Soundgarden and Alice in Chains, while standards of heaviness shift historically so that former metal like stoner rock now counts as plain rock.

Manuel Bremer and Daniel Cohnitz run "St. Vitus Dance" and Sabbath's doom through the failure-prone history of definitions of art: Plato's imitation requirement cannot cover the Technical Ecstasy robots or Pollock, Tolstoy's expression theory falters because Iommi's sampled cough on "Sweet Leaf" was not felt emotion, and the institutional theory merely says art is what the artworld accepts. They adopt Levinson's historical definition, an artwork is intended to be regarded as past artworks are regarded, and argue via Dennett's "forced moves" that, unlike relativity theory, Sabbath's 1968 leap in artistic space was radically unpredictable yet became the objective standard of doom that Saint Vitus and Sunn O))) later extended.

Dennis Knepp finds Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy gods at the birth of heavy metal: the Dionysian is the intoxication Nietzsche says makes art possible, realized in Sabbath's Hamburg residencies, Bill Ward's banana peels, the cough that opens "Sweet Leaf", and the mosh-pit loss of self that cures loneliness through communal revel, while the Apollonian is the god of terrifying dreams and visions seen in Geezer Butler's black apparition at the foot of his bed, the origin of "Black Sabbath", and Iommi's ghosts and angels. He argues Sabbath only looks Satanic because Christianity turned the satyrs and old gods into devils, and he rewrites Nietzsche's aphorisms Sabbath-style ("Iron Man is dead, and we have killed him") to drive the identification home.

James Bondarchuk tests purist principles about which line-ups are really Black Sabbath with thought experiments: the Ship of Theseus, from Plutarch plus Hobbes's reassembled planks, fits poorly because Geezer Butler is no plank, musicians contribute irreplaceable style, and "original members only" absurdly entails a Bieber piano-cover band would still be Sabbath, while the legal-ownership reading collapses once fans admit Bieber buying the name changes nothing. He concludes the whole "is it still Sabbath without Ozzy?" debate is not a metaphysical question with a fact of the matter but disguised aesthetic judgment, he remains a purist because Bill Ward's brooding drumming on "Black Sabbath" and "Hand of Doom" are integral to the Sabbath Sound, while conceding no objective answer exists.

Wesley Cray distinguishes fragile line-ups from bands that persist through them and proposes three criteria for a band's identity over time, continuity (successive line-ups share at least one member, chaining across gaps), intention (the line-up directs its intentions toward being that band), and uniqueness (only one line-up per band at a time, as the Gorgoroth lawsuit shows). Applying them, Tony Iommi is Sabbath's only essential member since "Ozzy was fired" makes sense while "Tony was fired" would not, so most post-Ozzy line-ups really were Black Sabbath, though Seventh Star, Born Again, and Cross Purposes fail the intention criterion, and the 2006 Heaven and Hell reunion was Sabbath continuing under another name.

Mark D. White shifts the is-it-still-Sabbath question from metaphysics to ethics, asking whether bands owe fans a stable line-up when they keep the name. Kant's Formula of Universal Law permits the maxim "change members, keep the name" without contradiction, and the Formula of Respect forbids only coercion or deceit, using fans as mere means, so the real wrong is deceptive marketing, as when record-company pressure billed Iommi's solo project Seventh Star as "Black Sabbath featuring Tony Iommi" and sent it out playing "War Pigs" and "Iron Man". The Dio reunion's honest rebranding as Heaven & Hell passes the test, while fans, symmetrically, owe bands no loyalty and may legitimately love only one era.

Erich Christiansen reads the supernatural imagery of the first two albums as the worldview of powerless working-class Birmingham men, applying Marx's claims that social being determines consciousness, that capitalists are "privileged and idle gods" over the worker, and that religion is simultaneously an expression of real suffering and its opiate. On this reading the figure in black of "Black Sabbath" personifies foremen and unseen bosses looming like factory smoke, "The Wizard" and the Lucifer-seducer of "N.I.B." answer the desperate worker's need for hands-on power when prayer fails, and "War Pigs"' Day of Judgment for the sorcerer-generals is itself the opium fantasy of workers who cannot deliver justice themselves, with "Wicked World" naming the whole system.

Kevin McCain turns Ozzy's "Am I Going Insane?" into a lived version of Descartes' skeptical scenarios, the madman who cannot trust his senses, the dream argument, the deceiving demon, and asks whether Ozzy can know anything at all. Using inference to the best explanation, he argues the commonsense external-world view beats skeptical scenarios because it predicts experiences (drop the book on your toe) and raises fewer unanswerable questions, so Ozzy keeps knowledge in the no-answer and "no" cases, but if he has reason to think he is insane and everyone tells him "yes", his reasons are defeated and he cannot even know their answers, leaving him, like the rest of us, one testimonial crisis from the void.

Jacob Held uses "War Pigs", "Electric Funeral", and "Children of the Grave" to teach just war theory's two halves, jus ad bellum (just cause, last resort, proportion) and jus in bello (proportion and discrimination toward non-combatants), reading Sabbath as condemning unjust wars like Vietnam and atomic overkill rather than all force, with Ozzy's "Thank God for the Bomb" voicing deterrence. Citing Walzer on "even in hell, it is possible to be more or less humane", he argues pacifism functions as a vital moral check, and that the war on terror fails just war standards outright: it cannot be won, so any means, assassination, torture, reclassifying terrorists outside both soldier and criminal law, are disproportionate and morally bankrupt, exactly the war-pig behavior the song's judgment day condemns.

Robert Arp dismantles the caveman stereotype of metalheads, stupid, simplistic misogynists who club women, by identifying it as the fallacy of hasty generalization, while conceding kernels of truth: groupie lines in Bel Air, studies linking metal to reckless behavior, and male sexual predation grounded (he suggests) in evolutionary psychology. Against the "numskull" charge he points to Geezer's clever anti-war lyrics in "War Pigs", Sabbath's complex song structures, the Wagner connection via Iommi's tritone, and classical-trained shredders, notes Sabbath's songs about women mourn loss ("Solitude", "Changes") rather than boast of conquest, and closes with Rob Halford's point that metal relieves the pain of dysfunctional homes rather than causing it.

holes.name: Eschatology (the Last Things)
holes.what: The branch of Christian theology concerning the last things: death, judgment, apocalypse, and deliverance, exemplified by the Book of Revelation.
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire argument is that Black Sabbath's Satanic and apocalyptic lyrics are an eschatological imagination borrowing the literary devices of Revelation against the Cold War and Vietnam backdrop.

holes.name: Philosophy of Music (convention vs natural expression)
holes.what: The debate over whether music's emotional meaning (joy, sadness, evil) is expressed naturally and universally or is a convention of a musical culture.
holes.why: Chapter 13 hinges on this dispute: McIver argues the devil's interval sounds evil only by Western convention, against Schopenhauer's claim that music directly expresses universal emotions.

holes.name: Catharsis (tragic purgation)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics of how tragedy purges the spectator's fear and pity through sympathetic engagement with horrific events.
holes.why: Chapter 17's central claim is that Sabbath's darkest songs ("Black Sabbath", "Iron Man", "Paranoid") work as catharsis exactly as Greek tragedy did, making the darkness essential to their artistic value.

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's idea that the instances of some concepts (like "game") share overlapping, criss-crossing traits with no single essence or set of necessary and sufficient conditions.
holes.why: Chapter 18 argues heavy metal is precisely such a concept, undefined by any stylistic conditions and united instead by resemblance to its prototype, Black Sabbath.

holes.name: The Definition of Art (institutional and historical theories)
holes.what: The philosophical project of defining art, from imitation and expression theories through Danto/Dickie's artworld institutional theory to Levinson's historical definition.
holes.why: Chapter 19 tests each major theory of art against Sabbath and adopts Levinson's historical definition to validate the band's doom as art, and no philosophy-of-art concept exists in the taxonomy.

holes.name: Hasty Generalization (fallacy)
holes.what: The informal fallacy of concluding that all members of a group have a trait because one, a few, or even most observed instances do.
holes.why: Chapter 29's whole argument against the caveman stereotype of metalheads is that it commits this fallacy, and the taxonomy has no logic or fallacy concepts.
